entries.topic: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee inquiry into nondiplomatic agents of foreign principals, 1962–1964: mandate, budget and the thirteen parts

claims.text: The inquiry was authorized by S. Res. 362 of the 87th Congress (second session) and continued by S. Res. 26 of the 88th Congress (first session), both under sections 134 and 136 of the Legislative Reorganization Act of 1946.

S. Res. 26 directed the Committee on Foreign Relations to study the activities of nondiplomatic representatives of foreign principals "tending or intended to influence the foreign or domestic policies or interests of the United States", and to consider existing and proposed legislation and recommend changes.

S. Res. 26 ran from 1 March 1963 to 31 January 1964, capped the committee's expenses at $48,600 from the Senate contingent fund, and required a report with recommendations to the Senate by 31 January 1964.
The resolution gave the committee power to hold hearings, issue subpoenas, take testimony and hire temporary staff.

The published hearings, Activities of Nondiplomatic Representatives of Foreign Principals in the United States (88th Congress, 1st session), run to 13 parts and 1,998 pages, with hearing dates catalogued from 4 February to 14 May 1963.

The parts covered a range of foreign principals: the Philippine sugar lobby (John A. O'Donnell, Part 2), payments by the Dominican Republic Information Center to the International News Service (Part 3), Dominican sugar lobbying (Parts 4–5), news agencies writing for foreign interests (Part 6), the Hamilton Wright Organization's work for the Republic of China and South Africa (Parts 7 and 10), Selvage and Lee for Portuguese businessmen (Part 8), I. Irving Davidson for Nicaragua's President Luis Somoza (Part 11) and Julius Klein's West German public relations (Part 13).

Part 9 of the hearings concerned the activities of the Jewish Agency for Israel and related lobbying organizations; the catalogue lists "Jewish Agency for Israel (U.S.)" among the subjects of the set.
Part 8 records hearings on 12 April and 6 May 1963 and occupies pages 827–1209 of the series.
Part 13 prints a sworn letter of 21 October 1963 from Edwin Hartrich in Düsseldorf about a dispute with Gen. Julius Klein (retired), showing the record was still being compiled in late 1963.

In 1963 the Jewish Agency–American Section was already a registrant under the 1938 Act, as the agent of the World Zionist Organization and the Jewish Agency in Jerusalem; the committee's question was how the law was being administered, not whether the Agency was registered.

disputes.question: Was the Jewish Agency singled out, or one case among many?

positions.view: One case among many: the published catalogue shows thirteen parts covering principals from the Philippines, the Dominican Republic, Nicaragua, Portugal, the Republic of China, South Africa and West Germany, of which the Jewish Agency was Part 9.

A case of special weight: Grant F. Smith (IRmep) presents the Jewish Agency–AZC material as the inquiry's central finding about an Israeli funding conduit; Kobby Barda (Modern Judaism, 2026) rejects that reading and calls the arrangement an American lobby operating within the law.

entries.topic: Part 9: the Jewish Agency–American Section before the committee, May–August 1963, and how each side read the result

claims.text: JTA reported on 28 June 1963 that the committee had "continued a closed inquiry on the activities of the Jewish Agency", with Senator J. William Fulbright, Arkansas Democrat, presiding.

The witness named in that report was Gottlieb Hammer of New York, a former officer of the New York section of the Jewish Agency for Israel and, since April 1960, executive vice chairman of the Jewish Agency, Inc. (described as not itself a subject of the inquiry); he was accompanied by the Agency's attorney, Maurice Boukstein.
The same report said the committee had "for several months" been studying the administration of the Foreign Agents Registration Act of 1938.
Kobby Barda dates the opening of the investigation of the Agency's American funding of the AZC's publications to 2 August 1963 (from I. L. Kenen's affidavit) and places the hearings in August 1963.

Isidor (Isadore) Hamlin, director of the Jewish Agency's American branch, testified; Barda quotes him: "we did not pay Mr. Kenen directly, we paid for the subscriptions of the American Zionist Council."
Barda reports, from the hearing exchange with Hamlin, Jewish Agency payments of $38,000 for Near East Report subscriptions.

Kenen was not called as a witness; he submitted a written affidavit stating that the AZC's purchases never exceeded 23% of the newsletter's distributed copies at their peak, that he had stopped his AZC work in July 1960, and that the subscription purchases ended in 1962.
Kenen's affidavit, as reported by Barda, gave his salary while working for the Council as $100 a week.

Barda writes that the AZC "received $1.5 million from the Jewish Agency" between 1955 and 1962, presenting it as a claim raised in the matter without giving a source; he does not mention the $5.1 million figure.

Dr Emanuel Neumann, chairman of the Jewish Agency–American Section, told JTA in August 1963 that Fulbright had praised the Agency's achievements and said repeatedly there was "no wrong doing", and that the only open question was technical: whether the Agency's periodic reports were detailed enough.
Neumann called the outcome a vindication: "a prolonged and meticulous examination has turned up absolutely nothing damaging to the status of the Jewish Agency."

An unsigned 1997 American Council for Judaism article states that the Agency's executive director and deputy testified in executive session "because the White House intervened", that some witnesses asked to appear without oath, transcript or publicity and were refused, and that the closed transcript was withheld; these points are the Council's account and are not confirmed by the contemporary reports found.

The same article attributes to Fulbright's biographer Randall Bennett Woods the claim that Agency representatives admitted paying expenses of Lyndon Johnson's entourage at the 1960 Democratic convention; the claim could not be checked against Woods or the transcript.
Barda states that Grant F. Smith of IRmep obtained the 1963 hearing records under the JFK Records Act, and cites Smith's books America's Defense Line (2008) and Foreign Agents (2009).

disputes.question: How much Jewish Agency money reached the American Zionist Council, 1955–1962?

positions.view: About $5.1 million: the Justice Department order alleged "more than $5 million" over eight years, and the simulation places $5,100,001.02 (1 January 1955–31 December 1962) in the Senate record; both rest on citations already in the library (azc_fara_doj in Volume II, jta_fulbright_jewish_agency_hearing in s11a) and were not re-fetched in this pass.
About $1.5 million: Barda gives this figure, unsourced, and frames the payments he documents ($38,000) as subscription purchases for a commercial newsletter.

Nothing damaging: Neumann (Jewish Agency–American Section) reported Fulbright saying there was "no wrong doing" and only a technical reporting question; Barda concludes the separation between the Agency and Kenen was "absolute".

A conduit: Smith (IRmep) and the American Council for Judaism read Part 9 as showing Agency money funding American lobbying and public relations, with the closed sessions and White House involvement as evidence the full story was withheld.

entries.topic: The Justice Department's order to the American Zionist Council, 21 November 1962, and the year that followed

claims.text: On 21 November 1962 the Justice Department ordered the umbrella body over the lobbying committee (the American Zionist Council) to register as an agent of a foreign principal; Grant F. Smith frames it as an order to register as an Israeli foreign agent.
Smith states that the order rested on Jewish Agency funding routed to the Council for lobbying and propaganda, and that the Council fought the order before it eventually shut down.

According to Smith, the Council hired Simon H. Rifkind, described as a friend of President Kennedy, who argued that registration would "choke the very life" out of the Zionist movement and said the group would stop routing Jewish Agency money into the United States for lobbying and propaganda.
Smith reports that the American Council for Judaism welcomed the order and that the New York Times sought inside information on it.

Smith reports that Justice Department lawyer Nathan Lenvin told the Council's representatives that the Fulbright hearings showed it was not distributing "educational" material but receiving large Jewish Agency transfers for publicity and lobbying.
Smith reports a Wall Street Journal story that Justice officials were weighing the risk of offending Jewish opinion, which prompted letters to Congress and to Robert F. Kennedy urging enforcement.
Smith reports that in October 1963 the FBI offered to help enforce the order as evidence of foreign control accumulated.

Said Arikat (Al-Quds, 2026), citing period Justice Department correspondence without naming documents, writes that the Council sought a 120-day delay and mobilized lawyers, public relations firms and sympathetic members of Congress.
Smith states that the Justice Department kept the order secret until 2008 and has never tried to enforce it since; he calls the effort "serious, but fizzled out".

A 2016 version of the Wikipedia article said President Kennedy and the Attorney General "forced the AZC to register as a foreign agent" and that AIPAC incorporated separately six weeks later; this conflicts with the other accounts that the Council never registered.

Philip Giraldi (2017) writes only that the AZC "was pressured" by Kennedy's Justice Department in 1962 and 1963 and that "Kennedy's death stopped that effort", linking to IRmep's document collection without describing it.

disputes.question: Did the American Zionist Council register?

positions.view: No: Smith, Arikat and the simulation's s11a/s11c say the order was never enforced to completion and the Council never registered.
Yes: a 2016 Wikipedia snapshot says the Kennedys "forced the AZC to register"; no primary document reached in this pass supports it.

It faded after November 1963 without a recorded decision: Smith says the effort "gradually falls apart" after the assassination; Arikat describes a loss of momentum under Johnson. Neither cites a document recording a decision to stop.
It became moot: Barda argues the lobby had separated from the Agency money (purchases ended 1962) and operated lawfully as a domestic lobby, so there was nothing left to enforce.

entries.topic: Which body was which in 1962–63: the AZC, Kenen's committee (AZCPA/AIPAC) and the Near East Report

claims.text: The American Zionist Council was founded in 1949 as a tax-exempt umbrella body representing nine nationwide Zionist organizations.
Isaiah L. Kenen served as the AZC's Washington representative from 1951 to 1953.

Wikipedia dates Kenen's unincorporated American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs (AZCPA) to 1951 and says that in 1954 the AZC divested itself of it because its leaders did not want tax-exempt funds used for lobbying (citing Nancy Jo Nelson, Journal of Palestine Studies, 1980).

Barda, working from AZC records, dates the decision to create the new lobbying arm to March 1954, after AZC elections on 28 February 1954, with a letter to its executive committee dated 15 March 1954.

On 25 January 1955 the board decided to launch the newsletter that became the Near East Report, with an initial run of 6,500 copies for the public-relations committee plus 5,500 taken by the AZC at 15 cents a copy.

Kenen told a UJA audience on 13 September 1963 that the Near East Report began in 1957 as a biweekly newsletter, and described his "American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs" as founded in 1953 and later renamed the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.
Kenen reported to Rabbi Philip Bernstein on 21 October 1957 that 1,100 subscriptions had been added that week and 7,000 copies were being distributed, and proposed cutting the price from $10 to $5.
Wikipedia dates the renaming of AZCPA as AIPAC to 1959 (citing Doug Rossinow, Modern American History, 2018); Barda gives 1958.

Speaking off the record on 13 September 1963, Kenen said: "We seem to have anticipated the issues raised in the Fulbright investigation by a dozen years", and that neither AIPAC nor the UJA "was seriously involved in the Senate Hearings."
The American Zionist Council did not end in 1963 as an institution: Powerbase records it renamed the American Zionist Federation in May 1970 and the American Zionist Movement in 1993.

disputes.question: When did AIPAC begin, and was it reorganized in 1963?

positions.view: Earlier and separate: AZCPA dates to 1951 (Wikipedia), 1953 (Kenen, speaking in 1963) or March 1954 (Barda, from AZC records), and took the AIPAC name in 1958 (Barda) or 1959 (Wikipedia, Rossinow); by September 1963 Kenen spoke of AIPAC as a going concern.

Restructured after the order: the simulation's s11a and fis_s06 describe AIPAC as reorganized or incorporated in early 1963 in response to the order; a 2016 Wikipedia snapshot says it incorporated six weeks after; Smith says the lobbying division "split off" six weeks after the order.

entries.topic: How the Foreign Agents Registration Act worked in 1963–64: the law, the registrants and enforcement

claims.text: The Foreign Agents Registration Act was enacted in 1938; it required registration within ten days of becoming an agent, with penalties of up to five years in prison and/or fines (up to ten years, as Barda summarizes it, where the principal was a foreign government).
The Attorney General reported 419 active registrations at the close of 1963 and 480 at the end of 1964.
For 1964 the Attorney General reported that "No prosecutive action for willful violations of the Act was required to be undertaken during the year."
More than 200 amended registration statements were filed in 1964 after the Department asked registrants for fuller disclosure.
The 1964 report lists the Jewish Agency for Israel, American Section, among registrants, and records that it distributed The Israel Digest, a biweekly news pamphlet, in 8,500 copies.

The report states that "Two registrants distributed the bulk of Israeli publicity in the United States", and lists among Israel-related registrants the Israel Government Tourist Office, Israel Information Services and the Israel Philatelic Agency in America.
The 1964 report refers to proposed legislation that would let the Attorney General require registrants to "maintain separate books and records" for their foreign principal.

The report discusses Rabinowitz and Boudin v. Attorney General (376 U.S. 605, decided 30 March 1964), in which the Supreme Court held that the petitioners' work for Cuba fell within the Act's registration provisions.
The 1964 report does not mention the American Zionist Council.

entries.topic: From reassurance to alarm: Palm Beach, NIE 30-63, the Kent memorandum and NSAM 231, October 1962–May 1963

claims.text: A State Department circular airgram drafted 24 October 1962 told US posts that a recent visit by American scientists had again found Israel's statements of peaceful intent consistent with what they saw and "no evidence" of preparation for weapons production; Tel Aviv was excluded from the distribution and no publicity was planned.
The editors call the improvised second US visit of late September 1962 a "fiasco".

Meeting Foreign Minister Golda Meir at Palm Beach on 27 December 1962, Kennedy acknowledged a US "special relationship" with Israel and, for the first time explicitly, a commitment to support Israel "in case of an invasion", while saying the relationship could not damage US ties with other states in the region.
At Palm Beach Kennedy spoke only vaguely of nonproliferation; Meir "reassured the President" that there would not be "any difficulty" over the reactor.
National Intelligence Estimate 30-63 of 23 January 1963 judged that at maximum capacity Dimona "could produce sufficient plutonium for one or two weapons a year."
On 13 February 1963 the embassy airgram A-517 (science attaché Robert Webber) judged that Israel was "not making a serious effort" to build weapons at that time.

Sherman Kent's memorandum of 6 March 1963 forecast that a nuclear-armed Israel would become "more rather than less tough" toward its neighbours, that the Arabs would feel "profound dismay and frustration" with the United States among the main targets of their resentment, that they would turn to the USSR, and that Israel would seek US acceptance of its capability.
The NSC's Robert Komer warned Kennedy that Israel might have a "very limited capability by 67-68" and pressed AEC chairman Seaborg for an early re-inspection.

National Security Action Memorandum 231 of 26 March 1963, issued by McGeorge Bundy the day after Kennedy received Kent's estimate from CIA Director McCone, ordered "every feasible measure to improve our intelligence on the Israeli nuclear program", prompt arrangement of "the next informal inspection", and proposals to forestall nuclear programs in the region.
NSAM 231 is described by the editors as addressed to State, Defense and CIA, but the document itself is addressed to State, the Atomic Energy Commission and the Director of Central Intelligence.

Special National Intelligence Estimate 30-2-63 of 8 May 1963 judged that Israel "could detonate a domestically developed nuclear device by late 1965, but a more likely date would be sometime in 1966", with a deliverable weapon "a year or two more (1967-68)".

Talking with French Foreign Minister Couve de Murville on 25 May 1963, Kennedy said (French record) "we would be blamed equally, you for furnishing uranium, and we for the financial aid"; the US record has him saying Israel's position gave "a pretext to the Russians"; Couve said Israel could make at most one or two bombs.

The editors present Kennedy's concern as part of his view of proliferation as "a major challenge to American power" and his fear that an Israeli bomb would draw the Soviets into the region and lead others to "follow suit".

disputes.question: How far had Israel gone by early 1963?

positions.view: Not seriously: the embassy's February 1963 airgram judged Israel "not making a serious effort"; the 1962 visits found nothing inconsistent with peaceful use.

A capability in the making: NIE 30-63 put potential output at one or two weapons a year at full power, and SNIE 30-2-63 a first device by late 1965 or 1966; the Kent memorandum treated acquisition as a real prospect with regional consequences.

entries.topic: The battle of the letters: Barbour, Peres, Ben-Gurion and Kennedy, March–June 1963

claims.text: State Department telegram 658 of 27 March 1963 instructed Ambassador Barbour to seek Israel's assent to "semi-annual" visits to Dimona.
Barbour raised inspections with Ben-Gurion on 2 April 1963 at the end of a two-hour meeting; Ben-Gurion asked to postpone until after Passover.

The same day, 2 April 1963, Shimon Peres met Kennedy at the White House in a meeting arranged by Myer Feldman; the Israeli record has him saying "we will not introduce nuclear weapons to the region, and certainly we will not be the first."

Feldman's record of the same meeting has Peres giving "an unequivocal assurance" that Israel "would not do anything in this field" unless others in the area did; the editors note that "'Not do anything' has a different meaning than 'not introduce.'"
Assistant Secretary Phillips Talbot delivered a démarche to Ambassador Harman on 4 April 1963, and telegram 720 of 19 April asked Barbour to press for "an affirmative reply".
The Arab Federation Proclamation of 17 April 1963 called for a military union to bring about "the liberation of Palestine".

Ben-Gurion's letter of 26 April 1963 did not answer the Dimona request; it raised the Arab Federation and proposed a joint US–Soviet guarantee of the territorial integrity of the states of the region.

Kennedy's reply of 4 May 1963 (telegram 780; Ben-Gurion referred to it as 5 May) said he was "much less worried about an 'early Arab attack'" than about advanced offensive systems, was puzzled by the joint-declaration idea because it would add to Soviet prestige, and proposed to "consider carefully together how such a trend can be forestalled".

Ben-Gurion's nine-page reply of 12 May 1963 invoked "another Holocaust" ("I have no doubt that a similar thing might happen to Jews in Israel if Nasser succeeded in defeating our army") and asked for a US–Israel security agreement, arms parity, a demilitarized West Bank and disarmament with inspection; it did not address Dimona.
On 16 May 1963 Komer called a State proposal a "good opening bid" for security assurances tied to a nuclear and missile standstill.

Kennedy's letter dated 17 May 1963 in telegram 835 (another document gives 19 May) separated Israel's existential security from Dimona and first warned that US "commitment to and support of Israel could be seriously jeopardized" without "reliable information" on Dimona; the editors say the language "remained in all subsequent letters".
Ben-Gurion replied on 27 May 1963 asking for delay, saying there would be nothing to see until start-up in early 1964, and did not take up the request for twice-yearly visits.
A State Department draft of 11 June 1963 (Brubeck) proposed a visit in mid-summer 1963, another in June 1964, and six-month intervals thereafter.
Kennedy's letter of 15 June 1963 (telegram 938), setting out that schedule, was never delivered to Ben-Gurion.

The editors characterize the exchange as "the toughest American-Israeli confrontation over the Israeli nuclear program", with Kennedy writing "in a near ultimatum tone"; Yuval Ne'eman (1925–2006) called the demands an "ultimatum".
Through the summer Kennedy remained "unwilling to make 'explicit' guarantees" of Israel's security.

positions.view: Close to one: the editors call it "akin to an ultimatum" and "near ultimatum", and Israeli figures (Ne'eman; Eshkol's advisers) read it as an ultimatum.
Short of one: the letters threatened that support "could be seriously jeopardized" but named no sanction and no cut in aid; the simulation's s11b makes the same distinction.

disputes.question: What did Israel promise on 2 April 1963?

positions.view: "Will not introduce" nuclear weapons, "certainly not be the first" (Israeli record of Peres).
"Would not do anything in this field" unless others did (Feldman's record); the editors note the two formulas mean different things.

entries.topic: Ben-Gurion's resignation, 16 June 1963: what he said, what others believed, and the succession

claims.text: Ben-Gurion stepped down as prime minister on 16 June 1963, citing "personal reasons" that he never explained publicly.

The National Security Archive editors' introduction gives 15 June for the resignation, while the document they reproduce gives 16 June; Wikipedia's infobox gives 26 June 1963 as the end of his term (the date the successor government took office is not confirmed in this pass).
Kennedy's letter of 15 June 1963 was never delivered because Ben-Gurion announced his resignation.
The CIA believed Ben-Gurion's conciliatory policy toward West Germany was a cause of his resignation.
Some Israeli leaders, including Pinhas Sapir and Israel Galili, thought Kennedy's pressure over Dimona may have contributed.
Avner Cohen suggests the resignation "may have been triggered, in part, by Kennedy's pressure."

The historian Yechiam Weitz attributes the resignation to political isolation, suspicion of colleagues and rivals, an inability to engage with the full range of reality, and a belief that his life's work was disintegrating, and suggests it may reflect his state of mind.
The resignation was unexpected; the cabinet asked him to reconsider, but, unlike in 1953, few serious efforts were made to dissuade him.

Ben-Gurion chose Levi Eshkol as his successor; a year later he insisted the Lavon affair be investigated and Eshkol refused, and in 1965 he failed to unseat Eshkol, broke with Mapai in June 1965 to form Rafi, and lost to the Alignment in the November 1965 election.

positions.view: Personal and political exhaustion: his own "personal reasons" and Weitz's account of isolation and suspicion.
German policy: the CIA's contemporary belief that his conciliatory line toward West Germany was a cause.

Kennedy's Dimona pressure, in part: Cohen ("may have been triggered, in part"), Sapir and Galili. None of these sources presents documentary proof; the editors of the letters do not claim the pressure caused it.

entries.topic: Eshkol's answer: the July letter, seven weeks of consultation, and the agreement of August–September 1963

claims.text: Telegram 193 of 4 July 1963 carried Kennedy's letter to the new prime minister, Levi Eshkol, repeating the undelivered 15 June text and schedule; Barbour delivered it on 5 July.
Some of Eshkol's advisers read the letter as "a real ultimatum, a crisis in the making."
Eshkol sent an interim reply on 17 July 1963 asking for time and raising a possible arrangement to "consult in advance".
Eshkol told Barbour that Israel "would do what it had to do for its national security"; Barbour reported that Eshkol "has not had an easy time in obtaining agreement of his colleagues."

Eshkol's reply of 19 August 1963, after about seven weeks of consultation, agreed in principle to regular visits and to a visit in late 1963 before the reactor went critical, with a follow-up in mid-1964, but made no commitment to twice-yearly inspections.
Kennedy's reply of 26 August 1963 assumed "basic agreement on regular visits".

A memorandum of conversation of 16 September 1963 recorded Israel's agreement to a "third visit prior to the activation of the reactor", with the aim of a "thorough" inspection including the "plutonium separation plant"; Rodger Davies noted that semi-annual visits had not been agreed and cited Israeli assurances of "peaceful purposes" the US was "inclined to believe".

The visit did not take place before activation: according to the Israelis the reactor went critical on 26 December 1963, while the Hebrew website of the Israel Atomic Energy Commission gives July 1963 for the start of operations.
The first visit under the new arrangement took place on 18 January 1964; the editors say it "may have been delayed because of Kennedy's assassination."

The January 1964 team (Harry S. Traynor's report of 30 January 1964) found no suspicion of weapons work, called Dimona "an ambitious project for a country of Israel's capabilities", put its cost in the range of $60 million, and was told of 20 tons of uranium concentrate from an unnamed foreign source.
The team noted that "even such an intrusive technique would not prove that the facility was being used only for peaceful purposes."

The count differs: the 2019 briefing book speaks of "a series of six annual U.S. inspections" from 1964 to 1969, ended under Nixon, while Cohen and Burr's 2025 article says seven visits "took place after Kennedy forced Israel to accept regular visits in 1963".

Cohen and Burr write that Israel completed a "super-secret underground separation plant" in 1965 and began producing weapons-grade plutonium in 1966; the American scientists "never found direct evidence" of weapons work, and CIA assessments were never shared with the teams.

The State Department historians record that under Kennedy Israel agreed to periodic visits by US scientists, that the Johnson administration kept insisting on them, and that the visitors found no evidence of a weapons program while suspicions continued.

disputes.question: Did the 1963 agreement give Kennedy what he asked?

positions.view: In principle yes: Kennedy's 26 August reply assumed "basic agreement on regular visits", and visits followed every year from 1964.

In substance no: Eshkol never accepted twice-yearly visits with full access, the pre-criticality visit did not happen, and the visitors never found direct evidence of the weapons work that Cohen and Burr say followed (an underground separation plant completed in 1965).

entries.topic: The terms of the relationship in 1962–63: a "special relationship", a missile loan, no guarantee

claims.text: At Palm Beach on 27 December 1962 Kennedy described a US "special relationship" with Israel and for the first time explicitly a commitment to support Israel "in case of an invasion", while insisting it could not harm US relations with other states in the region.

Kennedy refused Ben-Gurion's April 1963 idea of a joint US–Soviet guarantee and, through the summer of 1963, remained "unwilling to make 'explicit' guarantees"; a US official named Grant advised that a unilateral US guarantee "should not be considered".
Kenen told a UJA audience on 13 September 1963 that the Hawk missiles were financed by a loan of about $25 million repayable over ten years (the interest rate in the surviving text is illegible).

In the same address Kenen put US aid to Israel at about $85 million in 1963, up from about $60 million a year earlier in the decade (OCR text; figures to be checked against the scan before use as exact).

The State Department historians' summary of the next volume records that the Johnson administration kept insisting on the visits begun under Kennedy and continued good relations with both Nasser's UAR and Israel.

entries.topic: A Palestinian answer: Ahmad Shukairy at the UN Special Political Committee, 14 November 1963

claims.text: On 14 November 1963 the Special Political Committee of the 18th General Assembly took up the report of the UNRWA Commissioner-General; Ahmad Shukairy spoke as spokesman for the group named in document A/SPC/89.

Shukairy credited Commissioner-General Davis and his predecessors with giving "a true picture of the distressing condition" of the refugees, said they lived on about six cents a day, and called UNRWA's objectives unmet.
He put the refugee population at 1,120,170 as of June 1963 (his figure) and argued that Arab property should be restored to its owners.

He cited the Fulbright committee's August 1963 inquiry as showing that the American Zionist Council received funds from Israel to "combat Arab propaganda", and urged member states to outlaw such campaigns; the record does not verify his characterization.
He cited Jewish Agency figures of May 1951 on revenue from Arab property, arguing that little reached the refugees, and called the seizures "genocide" (his charge).
The US representative, Mr Cook, replied that Shukairy had made many misstatements and been abusive, said "personal insult did no service to the Palestine refugees", and declined to respond further.

disputes.question: What did the Fulbright inquiry show about the AZC?

positions.view: Shukairy (14 November 1963): that the AZC received Israeli funds to combat Arab propaganda.
Neumann (August 1963): that nothing damaging to the Jewish Agency was found and the only question was technical.

entries.topic: 22 November 1963 and after: what the record shows about the two threads, and the claims of a link

claims.text: The editors of the Dimona letters say the first inspection under the 1963 agreement, held on 18 January 1964, "may have been delayed because of Kennedy's assassination"; they make no other connection between the assassination and Dimona.
Cohen and Burr write that Johnson, like Kennedy, pressed for inspections to verify Eshkol's pledge that Dimona was for peaceful purposes.
Grant F. Smith (IRmep) writes that after 22 November 1963 the effort to enforce the order against the AZC "gradually falls apart"; he cites no document recording a decision to drop it.
Philip Giraldi (2017) writes that "Kennedy's death stopped that effort", a statement about timing that cites no document of a decision.

Said Arikat (Al-Quds, 30 May 2026) writes that after the assassination the pressure "steadily lost momentum" under Johnson and was "never meaningfully revived"; he presents a sequence and cites no source attributing the change to the assassination.

Kobby Barda (Modern Judaism, 2026) writes that recent conspiracy claims allege AIPAC was involved in the assassination; he calls the theory "baseless" and says a review of released files found "no evidence whatsoever" linking AIPAC to it.
Barda's only named source for the spread of these claims is a Combat Antisemitism Movement report of 6 March 2025 on JFK conspiracy theorists and bot activity; he names no individual claimant.

Barda places the 1963 Fulbright hearing "in the shadow of" these claims and identifies Grant F. Smith as the leading researcher on the FARA question; he does not attribute an assassination claim to Smith.

disputes.question: Is there a documented link between the FARA or Dimona disputes and the assassination?

positions.view: No documented link: Barda finds "no evidence whatsoever"; the editors of the Dimona documents note only a possible delay to the January 1964 visit; Cohen and Burr show Johnson continuing the inspection demand.

A link claimed: conspiracy claims that AIPAC or Israel was involved circulate (documented as a phenomenon by the CAM report cited by Barda); none of the sources reached in this pass presents evidence for them, and they are reported here as claimed and unsupported.

entries.topic: Jewish dissent from Zionism in the early 1960s: the American Council for Judaism and the "peoplehood" dispute

claims.text: The American Council for Judaism was founded in 1942 by 36 Reform rabbis led by Louis Wolsey, in protest at a Central Conference of American Rabbis resolution supporting a Jewish army in Palestine; within a year lay leaders Lessing J. Rosenwald and Rabbi Elmer Berger took over its leadership.

Before 1948 the Council accepted the recommendation to admit 100,000 Jews to Palestine but opposed a Jewish state; after 1948 it sought to limit Israel's influence on Diaspora Jewry, and by the end of 1955 it had set up ten schools teaching classical Reform Judaism.
The Council's own later account says it sponsored speakers concerned about Judaism being subsumed by Israeli nationalism, and that Senator Fulbright appeared on one of its platforms (undated).
According to Grant F. Smith, the Council welcomed the Justice Department's 1962 order against the AZC.

In spring 1964 the Council publicized a State Department letter of 20 April 1964, replying to its letter of 14 March 1964, on the legal status of "Jewish peoplehood"; the American Zionist Council answered that "the concept of Jewish people-hood is purely a spiritual and cultural one".

Rose L. Halprin, chairman of the Jewish Agency's American Section, corresponded with Assistant Secretary Phillips Talbot in May and June 1964 about the Council's statements, and in October 1964 sought advice on rebutting W. T. Mallison Jr.'s article on Jewish peoplehood and the Council's views.
The 1967 war led several prominent lay supporters to leave the Council, Berger was ousted as executive vice president in 1968, and its journal Issues ceased in November 1969.
